doc.title: Joseph Daley interviewed by Monk Rowe, Utica, New York, March 18, 2018

title: Tradition within free playing
summary: The trio does not abandon tradition; Sam Rivers knew the standards.

story.theme_name: Teaching jazz: schools, students and advice to the young

blocks.x: I don’t know if this is a silly question or not. But —
There’s no such thing as a silly question. I taught school for 30 years, every student. I said there’s no such thing as a silly question.

Well, do you, as a trio and in the other groups you’ve played in, do you avoid playing things that are much more obvious and associated with let’s say less progressive music. For instance if Scott started playing a rhythm & blues type thing in a very particular key, would you join that or would you feel like I’m going to go another way with that, and then would Warren pick up that tempo?

Oh yeah. Most definitely. I mean the thing is we don’t abandon the history. Last night we did not do that. Because somebody else just mentioned the same thing. He said, “I was waiting for you guys to do a groove or something. You never did a groove.” For some strange reason we never — I mean every night is different for us but yeah, but the night before actually we got into a really [scats]. Yeah we definitely do. Yeah. We don’t, I mean you know if Scott starts playing “A Train” we’ll jump right into “A Train” you know or whatever. I mean the thing is we don’t abandon the tradition and everything. If we need to bring it out and use it, or the trio moves into that, but definitely not at least me, and all the musicians that I know that play so-called free jazz or avante garde jazz, we’re not anti-tradition. And if tradition comes into what we’re doing, we’re not going to just push it aside just to be different. It’s not about that. It’s about extending the tradition into what we’re doing and everything. And I mean because Sam, Sam Rivers played with Miles Davis, he played with Dizzy Gillespie, and he knew all the standards, he knew all the tunes and everything.
Well it’s not that much different than the transition from swing music into bop then. Those guys were expanding the tradition.
